## Statement

Let $Y$ be any closed connected oriented smooth three-manifold, with two actual pointed Heegaard diagrams and specified complete compression-disk systems as in the closed-manifold definition. Assume Countable Choice. Up to orientation-preserving ambient transports of the diagrams, their marked points may be identified with one point $z$. Each diagram can then be equipped with an auxiliary oriented unknot $K$ and a second point $w$ so that $K$ crosses its splitting surface exactly at $w,z$, each half is a neat trivial arc disjoint from its compression disks, and it has explicit simultaneous bridge witnesses. After further ambient transports fixing $z$, both diagrams have the SAME auxiliary $K,w,z$.

There exist Morse function and descending-field endpoints on $Y$ realizing the two transported diagrams up to attaching-curve isotopies avoiding both marks. Each endpoint has one minimum and one maximum on $K$, its remaining critical points have indices one and two on the respective sides of the middle level, and the two endpoints agree with one fixed function and field germ on a common tube about $K$. All other critical points and the actual lower stable and upper unstable compression systems are retained through the final common-germ modification. No hypothesis on the homology or fundamental group of $Y$ is imposed. This is auxiliary geometric data, not an analytic basepoint insertion or a comparison of Floer complexes.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] The input handlebodies are smooth regular neighborhoods of finite connected graphs, with actual complete compression disks and one basepoint off their boundaries. ([[def-hat-heegaard-floer-complex-of-a-closed-three-manifold]])

[F2] In a handlebody embedded in $S^3$, broad proper compression disks with ball cuts admit same-boundary neat replacements and actual standard smooth rounded cut balls. The replacement is supported in arbitrarily small disk-boundary collars and may avoid specified disjoint compact data. ([[lem-proper-compression-disks-admit-neat-witnesses-with-standard-cut-balls]])

[F3] Actual neat ball, compression and bridge data give adapted Morse endpoints on any compact oriented three-manifold with boundary. Their prescribed disks are tracked by the relative one-handle cocore comparisons. One-sided endpoints glue across a surface in any closed oriented three-manifold, changing attaching curves only by marked isotopies. Already adapted endpoints tangent to one marked circle admit a common protected germ on any such manifold. ([[lem-neatly-bridged-compression-data-admit-adapted-morse-endpoints]], [[lem-neat-marked-morse-endpoints-glue-across-a-heegaard-surface]], [[lem-adapted-knot-morse-endpoints-admit-a-common-protected-germ]])

[F4] A smooth auxiliary Riemannian metric exists under Countable Choice. Parameterized Euclidean local inverses, compactly supported smooth flows on a compact time interval and finite compact-set cutoffs are available. ([[cor-every-smooth-manifold-admits-a-riemannian-metric]], [[lem-choice-free-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-in-euclidean-space]], [[thm-compactly-supported-time-dependent-vector-fields-have-global-evolution-on-a-compact-time-interval]], [[lem-manifold-bump-for-a-compact-set-inside-an-open-set]])

[A1] Only Countable Choice is assumed. All chart, graph, collar and handle selections added below are finite. ([[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** The data and Countable Choice in the Statement.

1.1 Move distinct basepoints to a common point if necessary. In a connected manifold any two points are joined by a finite chain of coordinate balls: the points reachable by such a chain form an open set whose complement is also open. Inside each ball join successive centers by a smooth coordinate path with compact interior track. A smooth time-dependent field equal to its velocity on a small neighborhood of the moving point, extended by a cutoff, transports that point by its flow. A finite composition gives an orientation-preserving ambient isotopy carrying one basepoint to the other. Transport its whole diagram, compression disks and splitting at the same time. This is an allowed embedded-diagram isomorphism, not a claim that its analytic action is the identity. Henceforth both basepoints are $z$. [F1, F4, A1, given, construct]

2.1 In a positive coordinate ball at $z$ straighten the splitting surface to $x_3=0$ and label its lower side $x_3<0$. Choose the ball disjoint from the entire finite compression-disk family: the disks are compact and none contains $z$, since their boundaries avoid it and their interiors are interior to their respective handlebodies. For sufficiently small $r>0$ put $$K_r(\theta)=(r(1-\cos\theta),0,r\sin\theta),\qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi.$$ Its two surface crossings are $z$ and $w=(2r,0,0)$ and are transverse. Its lower arc is oriented $w\to z$ and its upper arc $z\to w$. The two planar half-disks between its semicircles and the interval $[z,w]$ are explicit smooth corner bridge witnesses, neat at the surface edge. They miss all compression disks because their entire coordinate ball does. Each half arc belongs to the sole cut ball of its side. The full circle bounds the displayed planar disk in the ball, so it is an auxiliary local unknot with no global knot-type assertion needed. [F1, F4, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 The local round models from two positive charts based at the SAME $z$ are ambient isotopic fixing $z$, with their ordered $w,z$ and oriented circles carried along. Here are the germ and support details. Shrinking $r$ through positive radii gives an isotopy of the circle fixing $z$; a radial vector field, cut off outside a larger coordinate ball, extends it. For two coordinate germs fixing zero the transition $h$ is positive and smooth. The germs $h_a(x)=a^{-1}h(ax)$ extend smoothly at $a=0$ to $Dh(0)x$, by the integral formula $h_a(x)=\int_0^1Dh(sa x)x\,ds$. They are local diffeomorphisms on one uniform smaller ball, because their derivatives are uniformly close to the invertible $Dh(0)$. A positive matrix has a path to the identity: Gram–Schmidt gives a positive upper triangular factor, joined to its positive diagonal and then to the identity by straight interpolation; its orthogonal factor lies in $SO(3)$ and is a finite product of plane rotations. Thus the transition germ is joined to the identity through positive germs fixing zero. The velocity $\partial_a h_a\circ h_a^{-1}$ vanishes at zero. Extend it by a cutoff equal to one on the compact track of a sufficiently small model circle and zero outside the coordinate ball. The resulting flow fixes zero and agrees with the germ path on that track by uniqueness. Combine the shrinkings, this germ extension and inverse shrinkings. This carries one marked oriented local circle to the other while fixing $z$; $w$ is carried as its labelled other marked point. Carry each entire diagram and its disk and bridge data by this ambient map. We now have one actual $K,w,z$ for both endpoints. No simultaneous transport is said to preserve the old surface pointwise. [F4, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Prepare compression witnesses without assuming $Y$ embeds in $S^3$. Each handlebody is a smooth regular neighborhood of a finite graph. A spanning tree of that graph has a standard smooth ball neighborhood, obtained by repeatedly absorbing a leaf ball and its joining tube through disk collars. Every edge outside the tree supplies one framed one-handle. Conversely attaching these finitely many handles to a ball gives a smooth parametrization of the original regular neighborhood, by the same product edge and vertex charts. A ball with these finitely many handles has a standard embedding in $\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$: use disjoint small foot disks and disjoint arches, at distinct heights, for the remaining edges. Thus the abstract handlebody, independently of its embedding in $Y$, has a smooth parametrization into this standard model. Transport its actual auxiliary disks there, apply [F2], and pull the replacements and smooth cut-ball parameters back. This application is within $S^3$ only for the auxiliary model; it makes no Schoenflies assertion about a sphere in $Y$. Its supports may miss the local bridge witnesses, since those witnesses and disks were already disjoint in the local round-circle construction and remain disjoint after its ambient alignment. All attaching curves, actual arcs and surface marks are retained. The supplied complete system still cuts into ONE smoothly parametrized ball. [F1, F2, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 Apply [F3]'s one-sided construction to each actual cut ball with its single auxiliary arc, its explicit neat bridge half-disk and its transported face collars. It gives one lower minimum, the prescribed number of lower index-one points and their actual stable compression disks; the upper construction is dual. Glue them across the splitting by [F3]. The one-sided collar transports fix the surface, and the subsequent field interpolation changes the curves by its finite-time collar holonomy isotopies fixing $w,z$. Thus the endpoint diagram is the original transported diagram up to those allowed curve isotopies. Choose the ordinary critical heights distinct by the one-at-a-time finite handle order. There is no same-index trajectory: a lower index-one stable disk reaches the middle level as a compact disk and cannot terminate backwards at another index-one point; the upper assertion is dual. Index increase is excluded by the separated lower/upper groups and the empty outgoing or incoming spheres for extrema. [F3, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 Choose the auxiliary smooth metric by [F4] and use the common-germ clause of [F3] on the two resulting pairs, with the SAME actual oriented $K,w,z$ from the local-model alignment. Its ambient maps preserve $K$ and fix the marks. Transport the surfaces and disk systems too. At the final field blend choose its common tube smaller than the distance to BOTH finite compact transported lower stable and upper unstable disk systems. These systems are disjoint from $K$: its trajectories end at the protected extrema. The blend is therefore absent on every one of those actual systems and on all other critical charts. Each retained invariant disk still has its original local critical model; uniqueness of trajectories proves it is still the full truncated stable or unstable disk. No endpoint same-index trajectory has been introduced. The endpoint functions and fields now agree near $K$, with exactly one protected minimum and maximum and no other tube critical point. Every endpoint change has been an explicit allowed ambient transport or a marked curve isotopy. All auxiliary objects can be forgotten after a geometric comparison; no chain-map assertion has been made. [F3, F4, step 3.1, step 5.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $F/\mathbb C$ be a finitely generated field of transcendence degree one, and let $R=A_{\mathfrak m}\subset F$ be the local ring at a complex point of a curve, where $A$ is a finitely generated complex domain with fraction field $F$. Suppose $R$ is the actual DVR local ring of the given smooth point, with residue field $\mathbb C$, valuation $v$ and uniformizer $t$.

The derivation $D$ with $Dt=1$ extends uniquely from $\mathbb C(t)$ to $F$, satisfies $D(R)\subseteq R$, and for every $f\in F^*$ has
$$t\,\frac{Df}{f}\in R,\qquad \overline{t\,Df/f}=v(f)\in\mathbb C.$$
For $L,M\in F^*$ with $(v(L),v(M))\ne(0,0)$, the rational projective logarithmic ratio extends at the point with value
$$\left[\frac{\mathrm dL}{L}:\frac{\mathrm dM}{M}\right]_{x}=[v(L):v(M)].$$
The ratio of one-forms means their two coefficients in any common nonzero basis of $\Omega^1_{F/\mathbb C}$.

In particular the nonzero-valuation condition always holds when $F=\mathbb C(Y)$ for an irreducible affine curve $Y\subset(\mathbb C^*)^2$ with coordinate functions $M,L$, its normalization $U$ is the given dense affine open of a separated smooth completion $C$, and $x\in C\setminus U$ is an ideal point with the above local data. Singular affine branches retained in $U$ are not mistaken for ideal points.

For every finite field extension $F'/F$, an extending discrete valuation $w$ exists with residue field $\mathbb C$ and restriction $w|_{F^*}=e v$ for an integer $e>0$. More generally, suppose any field extension $F'/F$ is supplied with a discrete valuation $w$ restricting to $e v$ on $F^*$ for a positive integer $e$. Let a representation into $SL_2(F')$ have commuting peripheral matrices $\rho(\lambda),\rho(\mu)$ with a common eigenline of eigenvalues $L,M$. Use the valuation-ring lattice graph of [[def-adjoint-twisted-homology-and-culler-shalen-data]]. If the element $\rho(\lambda^a\mu^b)$ fixes a vertex or the midpoint of an edge, then
$$a\,v(L)+b\,v(M)=0.$$
For a primitive nonzero pair $(a,b)$ and a nonzero valuation pair it follows that the logarithmic projective limit is $[-b:a]$, the negative of the boundary slope $r=b/a$, including zero and infinity.

This applies in particular to a supplied equivariant map from the universal cover of a knot exterior to that lattice graph whenever a component of a transverse inverse image of the edge midpoints has a boundary circle representing $a[\lambda]+b[\mu]$. It does not assert that the graph is a tree, that such a map or an essential surface exists, that a character ideal point must be a peripheral ideal point, or that every possible boundary-elliptic surface choice has a prescribed slope. Those are separate geometric obligations.

## Statement references

[[def-adjoint-twisted-homology-and-culler-shalen-data|Actual ideal-point valuations, lattices and group action]]

[[thm-normalization-reduced-curve-exists-finite|Affine integral-closure normalization]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The fields, actual DVR local ring, uniformizer, finite-type coordinate algebra and, for the final assertions, the specified peripheral representation, extending valuation and equivariant inverse-image data.

[A1] Full AC is retained. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] A DVR consists of elements with nonnegative discrete valuation; every nonzero field element is a power of a uniformizer times a unit. The latter follows directly by dividing out its valuation. [[def-discrete-valuation-ring]]

[F2] The affine normalization is the integral closure in the function field. It is affine and finite, and a normalized curve has DVR local rings at its closed points. [[def-normalization-affine-variety]] [[thm-normalization-reduced-curve-exists-finite]]

[F3] A curve is separated; its diagonal is a closed immersion. [[def-algebraic-curve-over-field]] [[def-separated-morphism-schemes]]

[F4] Lattice vertices are homothety classes of free rank-two valuation-ring lattices. Matrix multiplication acts on vertices and edges. [[def-adjoint-twisted-homology-and-culler-shalen-data]]

[F5] The universal differential module represents derivations and is generated by differentials of field elements. [[def-kahler-differentials-algebra]] [[thm-kahler-differentials-existence-presentation]]

[F6] Finite separable integral closures of normal Noetherian domains are module-finite. Under AC a Dedekind domain remains Dedekind in such an extension; lying over supplies a prime above the maximal ideal, and localization at a nonzero Dedekind prime is a DVR. [[thm-finite-integral-closure-in-a-finite-separable-extension]] [[cor-integral-closure-of-a-dedekind-domain-in-a-finite-separable-extension]] [[thm-lying-over]] [[lem-dedekind-localisation-at-nonzero-prime-is-dvr]]

## Proof

1.1 **The actual field derivation.** The uniformizer is not constant: nonzero complex constants have valuation zero, whereas $v(t)=1$. It is transcendental over the algebraically closed field $\mathbb C$. Transcendence degree one and finite generation imply that $F/\mathbb C(t)$ is finite: finitely many field generators are algebraic, hence give a finite algebraic tower. In characteristic zero each tower minimal polynomial $p(T)=\sum_jc_jT^j$ is separable. If its root is $\alpha$, the preceding derivation extends uniquely by $$D\alpha=-\frac{\sum_j(Dc_j)\alpha^j}{p'(\alpha)}.$$ Here $p'(\alpha)\ne0$ since a nonzero derivative of smaller degree cannot share a root with the irreducible $p$. The product rule with this value preserves the relation $p(\alpha)=0$, so it defines a derivation on the quotient field, and uniqueness follows by differentiating that same relation. Induction gives $D$ on $F$. Differentiating these finite equations in [F5] also expresses every differential as a multiple of $\mathrm dt$. The derivation takes $\mathrm dt$ to $1$, so $\Omega^1_{F/\mathbb C}=F\,\mathrm dt$ and $\mathrm df=(Df)\mathrm dt$. [F1, F5, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 **A peripheral ideal point cannot have two unit coordinates.** Let $A_0=\mathbb C[Y]$, generated by $M,M^{-1},L,L^{-1}$, and let $B$ be its integral closure in $F$, so $U=\operatorname{Spec}B$ by [F2]. If $v(M)=v(L)=0$, then $A_0\subseteq R$. For $b\in B$, a monic integral equation over $A_0$ implies $v(b)\ge0$: if it were negative, its leading power would have strictly smaller valuation than every other term and could not cancel. Thus $B\subseteq R$. This gives a morphism $\operatorname{Spec}R\to U\hookrightarrow C$. It agrees at the generic point with the canonical local-ring morphism $\operatorname{Spec}R\to C$, since both induce the identity of $F$. By [F3], the inverse image of the closed diagonal under their pair is closed and contains the dense generic point of $\operatorname{Spec}R$, so it contains its closed point too. The two closed-point images are equal. The canonical one is $x$, while the other lies in $U$, contradicting $x\notin U$. Hence the valuation pair is nonzero. This argument uses normalization and separatedness, without assuming a singular affine curve itself is an open subset of a smooth completion. [F1, F2, F3, given, construct, algebra]

1.3 **The finite representation field admits an actual extending valuation.** Every nonzero ideal of $R$ is generated by an element of least nonnegative valuation: dividing any other element by that generator stays in $R$. Thus $R$ is Noetherian. A fraction integral over $R$ cannot have negative valuation, because its monic equation would have one uniquely least-valuation term. Hence $R$ is integrally closed. Its only nonzero prime is $(t)$, since a nonzero prime contains a power of $t$ and therefore $t$ itself; thus $R$ is Dedekind. For a finite $F'/F$, characteristic zero gives separability. Let $S_0$ be the integral closure of $R$ in $F'$. By [F6] it is finite and Dedekind, and some prime $\mathfrak q$ lies above $(t)$. It is nonzero because it contains $t$. The ring $S=(S_0)_{\mathfrak q}$ is a DVR. Its fraction field is $F'$: scaling each member of a finite $F$-basis of $F'$ by a common denominator in its monic equation makes it integral, as in the actual finite-closure proof. The residue field is a finite extension of $R/(t)=\mathbb C$, hence is $\mathbb C$. Write $w$ for the normalized valuation of $S$. Then $e=w(t)>0$, and every unit of $R$ stays a unit in $S$ since its inverse remains in $R$. Writing $f=t^n u$ proves $w(f)=en=e v(f)$ on $F^*$. This constructs the required extension rather than postulating a valuation on the model field. [F1, F6, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 **A finite bound proves local regularity.** Write $A=\mathbb C[z_1,\ldots,z_s]$ and take $$N=\max\bigl(\{0\}\cup\{-v(Dz_i):Dz_i\ne0\}\bigr).$$ All $z_i$ have nonnegative valuation. Differentiating any polynomial in them therefore gives valuation at least $-N$. Every element of $R=A_{\mathfrak m}$ is $p/q$ with $p,q\in A$ and $q\notin\mathfrak m$, so $v(q)=0$ and the quotient rule gives the uniform bound $v(Dh)\ge-N$ for every $h\in R$ with $Dh\ne0$. Repeatedly subtract the residue in $\mathbb C$ and divide by $t$ to obtain the finite exact expansion $$h=c_0+c_1t+\cdots+c_Nt^N+t^{N+1}h_{N+1},\qquad h_{N+1}\in R.$$ Its derivative is the polynomial derivative plus $(N+1)t^Nh_{N+1}+t^{N+1}Dh_{N+1}$. The first two terms are in $R$ and the last has valuation at least $1$. Thus $Dh\in R$ for every $h\in R$. This proves the needed regularity instead of presuming that a field derivation automatically preserves the local ring. The expansion uses only finitely many uniquely defined residues. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 **The logarithmic residue is the valuation.** For $f=t^nu$ with $u\in R^*$ and $n=v(f)\in\mathbb Z$, the product and inverse rules give $$t\,Df/f=n+t\,Du/u.$$ By step 2.1 the second term belongs to the maximal ideal $(t)$, giving the stated reduction. Apply this to $L,M$. Multiplication by $t$ gives a representative of their logarithmic ratio in $R^2$ whose reduction is $(v(L),v(M))$. When that pair is nonzero at least one coordinate is a unit, so the pair defines a regular projective map at the point and evaluates to $[v(L):v(M)]$. Changing the uniformizer or the basis of the one-dimensional differential space rescales the generic pair and leaves the projective value unchanged. On a complex algebraic curve this regular value is also the complex limit, since regular affine coordinate ratios with nonzero denominator are continuous. Cases with either one valuation zero are included and no division by that valuation has been made. [F1, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 **A fixed lattice forces zero eigenvalue valuation.** Put $A=\rho(\lambda^a\mu^b)$ and $\alpha=L^aM^b$. If $A$ fixes a lattice vertex, there is a lattice $\Lambda$ and $c\in(F')^*$ with $A\Lambda=c\Lambda$. Taking its top exterior lattice and using $\det A=1$ gives $2w(c)=0$. Thus $c$ is a valuation-ring unit and $A\Lambda=\Lambda$. In a lattice basis, $A$ has integral entries and its characteristic polynomial is $T^2-\operatorname{tr}(A)T+1$. An eigenvalue $\alpha$ of negative valuation is impossible: the squared term has strictly smaller valuation than the other two terms. Positive valuation is impossible as well, because $\alpha^{-1}$ is the other eigenvalue and has negative valuation. Hence $w(\alpha)=0$. If $A$ fixes an edge midpoint, it preserves that edge and possibly swaps its endpoints; $A^2$ fixes a vertex. Applying the same argument to $A^2$ gives $w(\alpha^2)=0$ and again $w(\alpha)=0$. Therefore $0=w(L^aM^b)=e(a v(L)+b v(M))$, proving the relation. For a primitive pair and a nonzero valuation pair its orthogonal line is exactly $\mathbb Q(-b,a)$, so step 3.1 gives $[v(L):v(M)]=[-b:a]$. This includes $a=0$ or $b=0$. [F1, F4, step 3.1, given, construct, algebra]

5.1 **The boundary loop of an actual inverse image fixes its midpoint.** Lift a boundary circle of the supplied surface to the universal cover. Its image under the supplied continuous equivariant map lies in the discrete set of edge midpoints, hence is one midpoint along this connected lifted curve. A deck transformation representing its loop therefore fixes that midpoint by equivariance. Moving the boundary basepoint to the marked peripheral basepoint conjugates the element and the fixed midpoint together, so $\rho(\lambda^a\mu^b)$ itself fixes an edge midpoint after that transport. Step 4.1 applies. No incompressibility, boundary incompressibility, transversality existence, or production of the surface has been deduced here; the result is the explicit boundary calculation for the supplied actual dual-map witness. [F4, given, step 4.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Any two actual pointed Heegaard diagrams of the same closed connected oriented smooth three-manifold are related by a finite sequence of attaching-curve isotopies and same-system handleslides avoiding the basepoint, genus stabilizations and destabilizations in basepoint-disjoint disks, and orientation-preserving embedded-diagram isomorphisms carrying the two handlebodies, surface, attaching systems and basepoint. Genus zero and empty attaching systems are included. The input compression witnesses may be proper in the broad smooth sense without boundary transversality.

Every intermediate diagram is a complete pointed Heegaard diagram of that same manifold: a genus-$g$ surface with $g$ disjoint compression disks cutting each handlebody into one ball. The theorem is purely geometric. It does not assert admissibility of every intermediate diagram, analytic maps, auxiliary-choice invariance, gradings or a comparison of complexes. No knot or extra basepoint is required in the input or retained in the conclusion.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] The closed pointed-diagram convention and its actual complete disk systems are supplied. An auxiliary local unknot through the basepoint gives two marked crossings, endpoint Morse pairs on the actual general manifold, and a common protected function and field germ, retaining the endpoint systems up to marked transports and isotopies. ([[def-hat-heegaard-floer-complex-of-a-closed-three-manifold]], [[lem-based-heegaard-splittings-admit-a-common-auxiliary-protected-unknot]])

[F2] On any compact closed smooth manifold the relative function construction protects fixed quadratic extrema by excising their balls, gives finitely many folds and ordinary value crossings, and keeps the remaining critical values in a uniform interior range. The actual general-manifold weak-field supplier then gives no index-increasing trajectory, finitely many isolated parameter-transverse same-index trajectories and product folds with whole event-free neighborhoods. The general-three-manifold grouping supplier retains these fields and the protected tube and separates indices at the middle level. ([[lem-relative-function-event-paths-preserve-fixed-extrema]], [[lem-cc-relative-descending-paths-have-finite-same-index-events]], [[lem-finite-weak-knot-morse-movies-admit-relative-middle-level-grouping]])

[F3] Ordinary clusters without connecting trajectories admit relative parameterized height rearrangements with the SAME field. Local quadratic handles and finite collar gluing retain their actual coordinate core and cocore and framed attaching maps. Product folds have their actual full crossing spheres meeting once. A single transverse framed cancelling pair can be removed relative to the incoming boundary, carrying subsequent attaching data. ([[lem-two-regular-critical-clusters-rearrange-parametrically-relative-a-knot]], [[lem-local-morse-sublevel-pair-is-a-handle-pair]], [[lem-gluing-handle-morse-models-along-collars]], [[lem-simple-function-births-admit-geometrically-cancelling-gradient-data]], [[thm-handle-cancellation]])

[F4] A smooth auxiliary Riemannian metric exists under Countable Choice. Parameterized local inverses, smooth Jordan-disk maps with prescribed boundary collars, supported neat proper isotopy extension, compactly supported flows and finite compact-set cutoffs are supplied. All applications to cut manifolds below follow finite rounding in product face collars. ([[cor-every-smooth-manifold-admits-a-riemannian-metric]], [[lem-choice-free-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-in-euclidean-space]], [[lem-smooth-jordan-disk-boundary-maps-extend-to-diffeomorphisms]], [[lem-supported-neat-proper-isotopies-extend-boundary-preservingly]], [[thm-compactly-supported-time-dependent-vector-fields-have-global-evolution-on-a-compact-time-interval]], [[lem-manifold-bump-for-a-compact-set-inside-an-open-set]])

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed as in the actual general-manifold suppliers. The additional disk, graph and event constructions are finite. No three-sphere move-generation or automatic-admissibility conclusion is a premise. ([[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** The data and Countable Choice in the Statement.

1.1 Apply [F1] to the two input diagrams. We obtain one auxiliary marked oriented circle $K$ with marks $w,z$ and endpoint Morse pairs on the actual $Y$, with precisely one protected minimum and maximum, and no other critical point on their common protected tube. The lower and upper systems are their actual stable and unstable systems up to the already specified transports and marked isotopies; the final tube blend was chosen to miss both compact systems. The endpoints have no same-index or index-increasing trajectory. Apply [F2]'s protected-extrema function path, its actual weak descending-field path and its grouping, in that order. These are genuinely general-manifold Statements. They give one finite movie fixed on a smaller common tube, stationary at the original endpoints. Its middle level is regular except at finitely many index-$(1,2)$ folds. Lower ordinary values are in separated ranges near $1/10,3/10$ and upper values near $7/10,9/10$; fold blocks have centers $1/5,1/2,4/5$. Near stationary endpoints the original grouped values are retained. No extra marked-pair insertion has occurred. [F1, F2, A1, given, construct]

2.1 Extract the actual disks on any regular slice with no same-index trajectory. Within the lower half reorder minima below the index-one points using [F3]: every inverted zero/one pair has no connection in either direction, since the only height-allowed direction would increase index. Finite adjacent exchanges decrease the inversion number. This is auxiliary bookkeeping with the SAME field, no change near the middle level or protected tube, and no change to stable sets. The upper procedure is dual. At a regular level between the zero- and one-handle groups, the sublevel is a finite union of standard quadratic minimum balls expanded through a critical-free collar. Each lower index-one unstable core has two distinct finite-time feet on these balls. An infinite transit would give a broken trajectory to another index-one point, prohibited here. Distinct cores cannot intersect by uniqueness of flow. The local handle comparison [F3] therefore gives the actual lower sublevel as those balls with framed one-handles at the feet. Its stable disks are the coordinate cocores $u=0$ continued to the middle level. Reverse hitting is finite: any break before that level could only be at another lower index-one point, because there is no lower index-two point. The cocores are disjoint, since a point has only one forward limit. Cutting them leaves the minimum balls with absorbable half-handle disk collars, hence actual standard balls. This is a finite handle description inside $Y$, not a claim about arbitrary embedded spheres in $Y$. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 The one protected lower minimum ball contains exactly the lower arc of $K$; every other ball is empty. In a small quadratic minimum sphere its two knot branches are antipodal radial rays. The finitely many pulled-back one-handle feet avoid those poles: a foot at a pole would be the same trajectory as a knot branch by uniqueness. Choose a meridian semicircle through the poles missing all foot centers, then take their foot disks small enough to miss this semicircle. Its radial half-disk is a bridge witness. Continue its boundary collar through the regular complement and absorb the cut half-handle caps; none meets that witness. The upper construction is the same with $1-f,-X$. Thus every slice gives extended systems with ONE occupied ball and possibly $e_0$ lower and $e_3$ upper empty balls. The lower zero/one graph is connected: all remaining handles have index at least two and connected attaching regions, so cannot join different components; the completed $Y$ is connected. The upper graph is connected by reversal. A spanning tree joins its balls into one ball; each remaining one-handle adds one to the boundary genus without disconnecting it. Consequently the middle level is connected and, with genus $g$, the extended system sizes are $g+e_0$ and $g+e_3$. Both sides are handlebodies. No homology assumption about $Y$ was used. [F3, F4, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Reduce an extended system to a complete system. Its finite connected dual graph has a distinguished occupied root. Choose a spanning tree rooted there and delete the disks corresponding to its edges. Regluing a leaf ball along its single joining disk absorbs a boundary disk collar, so a finite tree of balls is a ball. The retained system therefore has $g$ disks and cuts into ONE ball with the same protected arc and witness. For two trees, add an edge of the second absent from the first, remove an edge on its unique cycle absent from the second, and repeat; each exchange increases their shared edges. One exchange detaches an EMPTY tree component $E$. Glue its internal tree faces to obtain an empty ball. Its boundary contains the old joining face $a$, the new joining face $b$ and finitely many other retained faces. The complement of $a$ is a planar disk with these face holes and no marks. Slide the retained disk at $b$ over the other face holes successively, using thin bands in that planar region. Each band merges two face rims; after all mergers the new $b$ rim and $a$ cobound an empty annulus, giving a curve isotopy from the new disk boundary to $a$. The actual band sum is a parallel copy of the two proper disks joined by the band, pushed into this cut ball and rounded in its product collars. The remaining empty cap gives its proper-disk comparison to the $a$ face. A repeated retained label can have two faces in $E$; process them separately, always with the distinct anchor label $b$. No occupied arc or mark is in $E$. Thus a tree exchange is finite based disk slides and isotopies, not a homology computation. [F3, F4, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 This reduction also carries extended slides and empty cut-ball refinements to finite based slides. For an extended slide $D_b\mapsto D_b'$ over $D_c$, choose thin parallel disks and a band collar so the completed $D_b'$ is disjoint from the entire old family. Cutting along the old family, it is parallel to the boundary cap enclosing the two selected faces and their band; this cap contains no mark. Adding it splits off one empty ball, producing a common refinement of the old and slid systems. A tree reduction of either system lifts to a tree of this refinement by including the edge of the disk removed to recover it. The tree-exchange construction relates these reductions. For an insertion splitting a cut ball into an old ball and an empty companion, simply include the new edge in the lifted tree. Deletions reverse this operation. All these are statements about the ACTUAL CUT balls; no new disk is assumed boundary-parallel in the uncut handlebody. Empty or genus-zero complete systems cause no exception: their connected graph is a tree and deleting it leaves the single occupied ball. [F3, F4, step 4.1, construct]

5.2 On an event-free closed interval the actual middle levels and disks vary smoothly. Local critical models vary smoothly, and their compact crossing circles have uniformly bounded hitting times to the middle level: a divergent sequence would, by [F2]'s uniform broken-trajectory extraction, give a same-index connection at a limiting parameter. Scalar positive-speed regular models near a fold have the same invariant coordinate disks and uniform exponential hitting estimates on such a closed interval. Continue their cocores by those finite flows. Identify the levels by the supported field $V_t=-(\partial_tf_t)\operatorname{grad}f_t/|\operatorname{grad}f_t|^2$ near their compact regular union. It is zero near $K$, so the identification fixes $w,z$ and their knot germs. Transport a chosen spanning tree and its reductions. In the identified surface each resulting disjoint circle system is a smooth isotopy avoiding the marks. On a sufficiently small time subinterval its curves are graphs in disjoint annuli missing the marks; interpolate the graphs one at a time. A finite subcover gives finitely many allowed one-curve isotopies. Alternative endpoint trees are handled by the tree-exchange construction. No finiteness of other equal critical values introduced by grouping is needed. [F2, F3, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 Consider a single same-index event. Only indices one and two are possible, since a minimum has no outgoing sphere and a maximum no incoming sphere. For index one let $p\to q$ be its orbit, and use a small product block at $p$ with $f=f(p)-x^2+y^2+z^2$ and descending field $(2x,-2y,-2z)$. The event uses the positive $x$ branch. On the outgoing face $x=\eta$ the stable sheet of $q$, pulled back through a finite regular event tube, is a smooth curve $y=a(t,z)$ with $a(0,0)=0$ and $a_t(0,0)\ne0$. Write $a(t,z)=A(t)+zB(t,z)$. The section shear $(y,z)\mapsto(y-zB(t,z),z)$ straightens it to $y=A(t)$ and fixes zero. Its radial lift is smooth: for any such shear $H$, $$H(r\theta)=rL(r,\theta),\quad L=\int_0^1 DH(sr\theta)\theta\,ds,$$ so the lift is $(r,\theta)\mapsto(r|L|,L/|L|)$ on a smaller cylinder, with $L\ne0$. It changes the actual incoming collars only by supported smooth isotopies. Use $A$ as the parameter. The original quadratic flow has invariants $xy,xz$; its backward passage from $x=\eta$ to $|(y,z)|=\eta$ gives $x_{\rm in}=|(y,z)|$ and $v_{\rm in}=\eta v/|v|$. Hence the varying sheet is $xy=\eta t$, $x>0$. Opposite parameter signs round the same outgoing strip with complementary halves of the actual stable cocore $x=0$. The two quadrants have explicit smoothing graphs $|y|=\eta|t|/x$; fixing the outer collars and using monotone coordinate $x-|y|$ compares any two positive smoothing sizes without passing through $t=0$. [F2, F3, F4, step 5.2, construct, algebra]

6.2 For a fold choose a small regular-ended height band containing its two critical points and no old one; the numerical grouping ranges give this uniformly. Old handles outside the band have finite smooth collar transport. In its product model $f_t=g(u,t)-|y|^2+|z|^2$, after reflection $g_{uuu}>0$. The full local crossing spheres of [F3] lie in the block and meet once. Record a critical-free comparison, to retain the ACTUAL exterior attaching data. On a small fixed $[-r,r]$ choose $\rho=1$ near its ends and zero near zero, with $g_u>0$ on its support. Define $$c_t=\frac{g(r,t)-g(-r,t)-\int_{-r}^r\rho g_u}{\int_{-r}^r(1-\rho)},\qquad G_t(u)=g(-r,t)+\int_{-r}^u[\rho g_u+(1-\rho)c_t].$$ At the fold $c_t>0$, and it remains positive on a smaller parameter interval. Thus $G_t'>0$ and $G=g$ near both ends. With a transverse cutoff replace $g$ by $G$ on an inner box. No critical point appears in its annulus: choose transverse radius comparable to $r$; its signed-square gradient is bounded below by that radius, whereas the added derivative is $O(r^3)/r=O(r^2)$, uniformly for parameter size $O(r^2)$. On the unoccupied side the convex interpolation is also critical-free. Patch a descending field unchanged outside the block. Old same-index trajectories cannot enter and return from this modified height band, since their endpoint heights lie in one old index group disjoint from it; index increases remain excluded by group order. This gives a regular comparison with the unoccupied slice, retaining every exterior collar and knot germ. [F2, F3, F4, step 5.2, construct, algebra]

7.1 The local same-index calculation is an actual DISK band sum. Cut the stable disk of $p$ at the diameter where the event strip meets it, producing half-disks $D_p^+,D_p^-$. The continuing sheet toward $q$ is a rectangular band from this diameter to the surviving part of $D_q$. The two parameter signs cap that band by the two respective halves. Attach a parallel copy of the WHOLE $D_p$ to the first disk along a parallel band. Pair its $D_p^+$ half with the old cap across their product collar and flatten that collar; its remaining half is $D_p^-$. Thus the second disk is the slide of $D_q$ over $D_p$, followed by a proper-disk isotopy, with framing inherited from the actual product block and event tube. Outside this compact tube all hitting times stay bounded; a failure would yield a second same-index event by [F2]. Other lower disks and the upper system therefore undergo only isotopies. The tube and band miss $K$, since its trajectories go to protected extrema; compact separation allows them to miss every other disk. For index two reverse $f,X$. The common-refinement construction then turns the actual extended slide into finite based complete-system slides for arbitrary endpoint tree choices. No global feature of $S^3$ enters this coordinate and disk-cap proof. [F2, F3, F4, step 5.1, step 6.1, construct]

7.2 For an index-$(0,1)$ fold every OLD lower index-one value is above its entire band. Its stable disk, continued backwards upwards to the middle level, cannot enter that band, so old disks vary smoothly across the event. After cutting those old disks the pair lies in one old cut ball. The new one-handle has exactly one foot on the new minimum ball, because its unstable zero-sphere meets the full stable sphere of that minimum once; its other branch goes to the old side. No old uncut one-handle remains in this component. Cutting the new cocore therefore leaves a new minimum ball with one half-handle cap and the old ball with the other cap. The new ball is EMPTY: the protected knot halves descend to the unchanged protected minimum outside the fold. Both are actual balls by disk-collar absorption. This is exactly the empty cut-ball refinement just analyzed, even when there is only ONE protected minimum and even when the new empty ball is not a leaf in the uncut handle graph. It inserts no mark. The upper index-$(2,3)$ fold is dual. These extreme folds are thus erased by complete-system slides and isotopies; no analytic or geometric MOS insertion is being assumed. [F2, F3, F4, step 5.1, step 6.2, construct]

7.3 For an index-$(1,2)$ fold, its new stable and unstable circles $a,b$ on the middle level meet exactly once and bound their actual disks in the product block, with the product framings. Isolate them by the following finite cleaning. For each other lower curve meeting $b$, take an intersection nearest the crossing $a\cap b$ along a segment of $b$ having no intervening old intersection. Slide that lower disk over the new lower disk $a$ along a thin parallel band on this segment. The two contact arcs near the endpoint cancel after pushing the parallel band through its disk collar, removing that selected intersection with $b$; disjointness from other lower disks is retained by choosing the band on the cut side and nearest the crossing. Continue, decreasing the finite intersection number. Now clean upper curves meeting $a$ dually using $b$. The second cleaning does not restore the first, since the lower curves now miss the whole band neighborhood of $b$. All bands miss $K$ and the marks, since $a,b$ lie in its disjoint fold block. The regular neighborhood of the two new framed disks after cleaning is the standard cancellation region: its surface part is a punctured torus with meridian $a$ and longitude $b$, and its boundary misses every other disk. In local crossing coordinates the single attaching/belt intersection is the product one; [F3]'s framed cancellation fills it by a disk and absorbs its boundary collar, relative to the incoming band boundary. In the critical-free replacement's scalar model the filled level is precisely the graph $G_t(u)-|y|^2+|z|^2=1/2$, since $G_t'>0$. Thus the cancellation identifies the cleaned old attaching arcs with their graph projections, fixed on exterior collars. They are the actual replacement presentation, not just a presentation of a diffeomorphic ambient manifold. Conversely inserting this framed pair in that disk is the standard genus-one stabilization. For completeness its local ball has an explicit product description: thicken the two distinguished disks on their opposite sides and the single crossing box, using their product collars. Each remaining disk thickening is a ball attached to that box along a disk face; absorption of these disk collars gives a ball. Its surface trace is a disk crossing chart plus the two alternating edge bands, hence a once-punctured torus. Thinness and the cleaned boundary curves make its boundary miss all other disks. After cutting either distinguished disk its half of this ball is an empty boundary cap of the corresponding cut ball. Existing bridge witnesses can be chosen to miss this cap: push each auxiliary boundary subarc out of the empty cap across its disk boundary, then extend this finite interval isotopy through a thin inward collar fixed near the marked endpoints and actual knot arc. Round its finitely many corners first; [F4] supplies the supported extensions. Thus the cut-and-cap replacement retains the one occupied arc and its bridge witness, and the exterior tree reductions still apply. This construction is local and requires no Schoenflies theorem for $Y$. [F2, F3, F4, step 6.2, construct]

8.1 Choose disjoint closed event intervals about all folds and same-index trajectories and finitely many event-free intervals covering their complement. The regular-interval, isolated-trajectory and three fold arguments give the actual extended-system comparisons on these intervals. For a middle fold choose identical exterior trees outside its local cancellation region; its disk-collar filling retains those exterior cut balls. This yields precisely one genus change on their complete reductions, with the finite cleaning slides. For extreme folds use the empty-ball and common-refinement arguments. At common regular endpoints any tree discrepancy is finite slides by the tree-exchange construction. At the original endpoints there are no empty balls, so the complete reductions are exactly the endpoint systems constructed at the start, up to their already proved marked isotopies. Concatenate the finite comparisons. Every retained system has $g$ disks and one ball on each side by the cut-ball extraction and tree reduction; local genus changes adjust both disk counts by one. Curve perturbations against the other system can be made transverse at the finitely many resulting diagrams, away from both marks, by small surface graph perturbations; they are curve isotopies and do not alter completeness. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 5.2, step 7.1, step 7.2, step 7.3, construct]

9.1 Finally FORGET the auxiliary $K$ and $w$ throughout this comparison. Every curve isotopy, disk-slide band and genus-change disk avoided BOTH $w,z$, hence is an allowed move avoiding the original sole basepoint $z$. The ambient transports used at the endpoints and on regular levels carry all the original embedded-diagram objects, so remain the permitted isomorphisms after forgetting. No operation on a Floer complex accompanies this forgetting, and no tensor factor or marked-pair comparison is asserted. Reversing the endpoint transports recovers the two original diagrams, including different initial basepoint positions as allowed by the point-transport construction of [F1]. The genus-zero case is covered by the tree reduction when no retained disks remain. All additional choices are finite; Countable Choice was spent only at the stated local, function and weak-field suppliers. The entire construction used connectedness of $Y$, finite handlebody data and actual local product events, never its being $S^3$, an automatic-admissibility assertion or an analytic move theorem. This proves the full geometric claim. [F1, F2, F3, F4, A1, step 1.1, step 8.1, construct] ∎
